newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin has "burning desire" to return to Kremlin.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin has "burning desire" to return to Kremlin.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, recuperating after a bout of pneumonia, is very keen to return to work but has still not recovered fully, his press secretary said on Friday.

"The president clearly has a huge, burning desire to return as soon as possible to carrying out his duties in full...and it is clear he has retained his characteristic political will," Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.

"But on the other hand the president has not fully recovered after his very serious illness, double pneumonia. His physical condition is not good enough to expect him to force his return to the Kremlin."
Asked if Yeltsin was overworking against the advice of doctors, the spokesman said: "Sometimes in the process of recuperation and healing he doesn't spare himself."
Yeltsin's chief doctor suggested earlier in the week that the president was ignoring medical orders and working more than the three hours or so he had recommended.

Yastrzhembsky said he had met Yeltsin on Wednesday when the president made an unexpected visit to the Kremlin. However, since Yeltsin developed pneumonia, his office has not released any photographs or videos of the president, even after his Kremlin visit to meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Doctors have said Yeltsin will need two to three weeks to recover fully from his pneumonia, which struck only two weeks after the president's return to work after heart surgery.

The spokesman said Yeltsin had met aides on Friday at the Gorky-9 country residence outside Moscow. They discussed next Monday's elections in breakaway Chechnya, Moscow's relations with NATO and the United States, and Russia's regional elections.
On Friday Yeltsin also appointed a deputy defence minister as his envoy to the Russian parliament as it reviews the START-2 disarmament treaty signed with the United States in 1993.
The parliament has not ratified START-2, and the agreement is unpopular among many deputies who believe it forces Russia to sacrifice its most modern strategic nuclear systems.

Yastrzhembsky said a February meeting scheduled between Yeltsin and French President Jacques Chirac still stood, but he avoided a direct answer when asked about a planned March meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton in the United States.
"Since the White House did not confirm it, it would be strange for the Kremlin to confirm it," he said.
